awd_titl_txt: STTR Phase I: Highly Efficient Photovoltaic Power Converter for Optical Power Beaming
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial impacts of this Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project are in addressing critical bottlenecks in the unmanned aerial vehicle, wireless power transmission, and semiconductor industries. The proposed laser power beaming innovation plays a pivotal role in establishing a power grid for remote provisioning of energy to devices. The proposed work is important for several industry verticals where physical wiring may not be a practical solution for continuous and clean power supply. The electric aircraft market has an immediate need for an alternative charging solution. Battery longevity remains a critical bottleneck in the drone industry, causing disruptions in usage and operational efficiency due to frequent and mandatory recharging procedures. This work targets expansion of battery capabilities through a far-field wireless charging solution which directly addresses the unmet needs of drone manufacturers and operators alike and allows for longer operational periods, greater flexibility in device usage, and increased performance capabilities. This project stands to contribute to the fields of photonics, semiconductor technology, and energy harvesting, providing a novel solution to a longstanding challenge in the electrical aircraft market through the advancement and application of wireless power transfer. The proposed innovation serves to drive innovation in the energy efficiency technologies, which are critical to national energy independence and technological leadership. 

This Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project aims to enhance the overall power conversion efficiency for wireless power transmission systems through the development of a highly efficient photovoltaic power converter. The proposed innovation is built on the concept of a one-way coherent absorber with inverse-designed aperiodic multilayer front- and back-reflectors that enable maximal optical absorption in a thin-film photovoltaic material for broad incident angles. Innovative design configurations and high-quality fabrication through molecular beam epitaxy will be employed to construct the device based on optimized multilayer binary mirrors, thus aiming to reach record-high external quantum efficiency by efficiently trapping monochromatic light for an oblique angular range. The proposed photovoltaic receiver, responsible for absorbing laser fluence and converting it to electrical energy, will realize substantial progress in power conversion efficiency for far-field power transmission. This approach, which integrates advanced optical and electrical characterization methods, promises to deepen the understanding of light-matter interactions at the atomic scale and has the potential to unlock new avenues for high-efficiency, scalable wireless power systems.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This NSF STTR Phase I award advanced the development of a gallium arsenide (GaAs) resonant-cavity photovoltaic power converter for long-range optical wireless power transfer. The research investigated whether coherent optical interference and engineered semiconductor cavities could enhance light absorption within a thin GaAs photovoltaic active region while maintaining performance across a broad range of incident angles.

The award established a complete resonant-cavity photovoltaic architecture and demonstrated significant progress in optical design, semiconductor modeling, epitaxial fabrication, and experimental characterization. The developed structure incorporates a binary multilayer reflector stack of optimized AlAs/AlGaAs, a thin-film intrinsic GaAs absorbing region, and appropriately doped semiconductor layers for intracavity electrical contacts. The architecture deviates from conventional back contact design by promoting lateral carrier transport, thus enhancing optical confinement while permitting electrical carrier extraction without requiring current transport through the multilayer bottom reflector.

Numerical optimization identified configurations with approximately 53.8% average active-region absorption over a 0–70° angular range. Complementary semiconductor simulations evaluated doping-dependent carrier mobility, photogeneration, recombination, and electrical extraction predicting a fill factor of 87%. These results established a preliminary electrical-performance framework and identified critical transport considerations for subsequent device fabrication.

Experimental accomplishments included successful epitaxial growth and characterization of optimized AlAs/AlGaAs reflector structures using molecular beam epitaxy (MBE). Structural characterization using scanning electron microscopy and high-resolution X-ray diffraction supported evaluation of the grown multilayers. Optical measurements demonstrated greater than 92% reflectance near the target operating wavelength across incidence angles extending to approximately 80°, providing experimental evidence of the engineered reflector's broad-angle optical response. Preliminary fabrication using inductively coupled plasma reactive-ion etching achieved a measured etch depth of 1.102 µm, establishing an initial processing benchmark for subsequent device integration. The project also established a laboratory optical wireless power-transfer testbed providing a foundation for controlled receiver characterization and future system-level efficiency measurements.

Furthermore, the broader impacts of this work extend beyond the development of photovoltaic power converters to strengthening semiconductor research infrastructure, advancing domestic photonics capabilities, and establishing a foundation for new applications of optical wireless power transfer. The technology addresses a fundamental challenge in long-range optical power beaming: efficiently converting incident laser energy into usable electrical power despite changes in receiver orientation and stringent size and weight constraints. Successful development could enable longer-duration unmanned aerial operations where limited battery endurance restricts operational productivity for applications requiring large area coverage. Beyond these potential applications, the award contributed to lasting improvements in the physical infrastructure of the molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) facility, including an additional aluminum effusion source, independent flux-control capabilities, upgraded shutter mechanisms, and equipment restoration supporting the growth of complex III–V semiconductor heterostructures. These improvements expand the facility's capabilities beyond the immediate project, supporting future research in photovoltaic devices, semiconductor lasers, photodetectors, and other advanced photonic technologies.

Overall, this NSF Phase I project established the technical foundation for a new class of resonant-cavity photovoltaic power converters designed to address a critical limitation in optical wireless power transfer: efficiently converting incident laser energy into usable electrical power while maintaining performance under varying illumination angles. The results of these efforts established a foundation for complete device fabrication, manufacturing scalability,  and integrated wireless power transfer performance. These capabilities are essential to enabling high-efficiency, long-range optical power beaming for mobile platforms, including unmanned aerial systems, where receiver orientation, available surface area, and payload constraints directly affect system performance.
